questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I primarily chose Sydney University due to the location, not the university itself. I have been to Sydney before, and I had friends and family there I really wanted to see again. The last time I was in Sydney I never got to really experience the city due to Covid, so I thought exchange would be a perfect opportunity to go back to see more of the city and the rest of Australia. USyd also has a good academic reputation and the weather is generally good in Sydney which were both bonuses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Already in the week before orientation week the uni held introduction meetings where they gave a bit of information about the layout of the campus, the events during the orientation week and what to expect from the rest of the semester. They also gave tips on which apps to get to make settling into Sydney and uni life easier.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We were all assigned a student adviser who could help us find answer to any questions we had about the university campus and orientation events, or more academic related question such as about lectures and signing up to different units. My adviser changed a couple of times which made it a bit confusing or hard to get a hold of them sometimes, and they generally took a while to answer due to them receiving many messages, but overall they were very helpfull.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It really depends on how picky you are or how high your standards are. I knew the different areas in Sydney beforehand, so I knew I wanted to live in either Newtown or Glebe which is walking distance from campus but also have a lot of stuff happening there in general. I arrived in Sydney the week before the orientation week to start looking for an room and stayed with family in the beginning so I wasn't in a rush to find something immediately. I was recommended to look on Flatmates to find a room in a sharehouse but I thought it was quite hard to find good places on the site and many of the places that looked nice on the pictures didn't in real life or were very overpriced. I preferred looking on Facebook groups (most are called 'sharehouses in (area of Sydney)') which was where I ended up finding my room in a house with 2 other local girls.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In many cases it's cheaper to find your own room in a sharehouse than student accommodation, but it's definitely also much more effort to do so. The only reason I did it was because I knew which area I wanted to live in and that I didn't have to worry about temporary housing before I found my own place. Otherwise I would have found it too overwhelming and stressful. If you want to find your own place definitely arrive early so you have time to decide which area you want to live in and go see the rooms/meet the potential housemates, as the general standard of the rooms on flatmates specifically for exchange students is quite low and clear that people don't treat the places very well. I preferred the homes where the other housemates lived there long term, as they felt more like homes and you got to meet more local people. Socially it would have been nice to live in the big student accommodation, QMB, but this also had its own down sides such as being more expensive, not having your own toilet/bathroom and only having one big kitchen for the whole building. Even if you live off campus it's easy to join the social events/parties at QMB as long as you know someone who lives there.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: After getting accepted to the exchange program we were sent a list of available units/classes during the semester we would be there. Initially we could chose as many units we wanted and the different faculties then had to evaluate whether or not we could take the units. From the list of approved units we had to choose 4 units to start out with but during the first two weeks of lessons you were able to drop/change units as long as it was approved by USyd and Copenhagen uni.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We only had our student adviser who told us about the process and had to process all our requests to drop/change units but she could not guarantee our requests would be approved or advise us on how relevant the different units were for our studies.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the first  round of unit requests many on my list were rejected due to 'lack of required prerequisites', but when I explained how I did have equivalent prerequisites most of them were approved. However, one of the units I wanted the most was never approved and another was cancelled a week before lectures started so I had to chose another one.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Two of the units I ended up taking were 3rd year level so it was meant to be an extension on material we had learned about before in units back home, but it ended up just being a repetition of the same material we had already heard about in previous courses and didn't add much extra. So overall these were not that high academic level even though they were supposed to be the highest level I took there. The other unit was lower level (2nd year unit) but was on a completely different area than the courses i've had back home, so it was a lot more challenging. Overall, the academical level felt a bit lower but I had to spend a lot more time on uni work due to assignments throughout the semester, rather than just having a final exam.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: To some extent I really enjoyed having the assignments throughout the semester as it took some pressure off the final exam and allowed you to test your understanding during the course. However, often they were also really time consuming considering the amount of marks you could actually get from the assignments, so I recommend getting started on them early. I really didn't enjoy the style of the lectures as many of them were still only offered on zoom or both zoom and in person, but only 15% of the student showed up in person which made it hard to meet people in the classes and was clearly frustrating for the lecturers. The lab sessions were also a bit of a joke a lot of the time. They had really good facilities but the experiments weren't planned that well and a lot of time were wasted during the the lab sessions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Learning in outdoor education EDUH4052
Microbes, infection and immunity MIMI2002
Beyond the genome BCMB3004
Biochemistry of human disease BCMB3003

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I highly recommend doing the Learning in outdoor education. It is a really good way to meet other exchange students as it's not even offered to local students and Wayne who runs the course was amazing. It was quite an easy course to do as there was no final exam, the course finished right after mid-term and most of the lecture time was used on two hiking trips to the Royal national park and the Blue mountains. MIMI2002 was also really interesting as it was mostly new material we learned about and the two women in charge of the course were very organised and had a great relationship with each other and their students. They were clearly interested in us learning as much as possible and always put in a lot of effort to explain extra stuff to us or share extra material for us to look at if we wanted. The only downsides were that all lectures were online and that there at times were a bit too much material to get through it all. Unfortunately this course will not be taught by either of them anymore, so the structure might change for future semesters. BCMB3004 was a lot of repetition from previous courses i've taken but Stuart who taught the course was really good. It was clear he was an expert in the field of proteomics and he went above and beyond to ensure everyone could keep up and were enjoying the course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were quite expensive, especially if you don't shop at Aldi, Coles or Woolworths and buy the store's own brand. Renting cars/campervans is also very expensive in general but if you're under 25 years old there's also an extra cost added due to insurance for young drivers.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The uni has a lot of clubs and societies that you can join such as yoga, bushwalking, cheerleading, rugby, debate, and many many more. Most of them are introduced at the societies fair in orientation week but others you have to hear about from other students. Some of the societies are free to join and others you have to pay a fee which is usually not that high.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The yoga society was really good and only cost 5$ for the whole semester.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely go to Melbourne, it's close and you can usually get flights at an okay price if you go on a weekend trip. In my opinion Melbourne had a much better cultural scene and nightlife than Sydney so it was nice to experience. I also really enjoyed going to Byron bay further up the east coast and travelling around the South-west loop in Western Australia (this is a lot further away though and tickets are more expensive). If you don't do the learning in outdoor education course then going to the blue mountains is a must, the Figure 8 pools in the Royal national park is also supposed to be cool but hard to plan due to the tides, and I never got to see Jervis bay but really wished I had time to.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, it's very similar to danish culture (very western) but has more beach culture and fancy coffee.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't meet many local students at the uni as most of them didn't show up to the lectures, so mostly I met locals through my housemates, at the QMB parties or through other friends that had met locals. Sign up to different societies where it's not only for exchange students and just start conversations with them. The local students don't seem as interested in making new friends as the other exchange students and aren't as inclusive so you have to put more effort into socialising with them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: there aren't really any that I found challenging

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The coffee, if you're not already a coffee addict there's a real risk you will become one. I also really enjoyed Australia's appreciation of nature and outdoor activities, I definitely think I'll try to go hiking a lot more in Denmark after doing it so often in Sydney.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Stay up to date with the assignments throughout the semester and get as many marks as possible from these as it takes a lot of pressure of the final exam (if you even have one).
2. Sydney doesn't only have great weather. We had sooooo much rain most of the semester there due to the weather phenomenon called La Niña, so don't only bring summer clothes and don't expect everyday to be a beach day.
3. Shop at Aldi, not Foodworks

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: .Don't stress too much about picking units you want to take before arriving. During the first 1-2 weeks you have the option to switch units if you find out your chosen ones aren't for you, if they're too difficult, too easy, etc.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the people I met! There were so many lovely people I shared my time and experience there with, that I know I'll continue to talk to and see even after leaving.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Staying motivated during the zoom lectures

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
